task.goal: Help a repair shop give accurate pickup estimates when parts arrival varies.
hard_constraints: Two staff, paper job cards and an existing supplier email inbox; no paid software.
Do not promise a date unsupported by parts status or hide delays.
Compare missed estimates, customer calls and staff time for four weeks.
task.available_resources: Past 30 job records and supplier replies.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Parts-status gates with a firm next-update commitment
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Replace a single pickup date with explicit evidence gates on each paper job card: ordered with no confirmed dispatch; dispatched with supplier arrival range; physically received and checked; repair scheduled. The mechanism is to prevent uncertain supply information from becoming a customer promise while giving customers a reliable time to hear next.

One staff member checks supplier email at two fixed times daily and records the latest status, its timestamp and the next check on affected cards. The other uses that entry when speaking to customers; both can cover either role. Before receipt, say, for example: “The supplier reports arrival Tuesday–Thursday. Pickup is still unconfirmed; we will update you Wednesday afternoon.” Offer a conditional pickup window only when supplier evidence and available repair capacity support it, stating those conditions. Once the correct parts are received and checked, assign a pickup window against the shop’s actual workload. Notify customers promptly when evidence invalidates a previously communicated window, explaining the cause and revised status.

Use the 30 past records to identify common unsupported promises and estimate ordinary repair time after parts receipt. Implementation requires only a handwritten status key, job-card fields, the existing inbox and a daily callback list. It assumes staff can reliably connect supplier replies to jobs and reserve realistic workshop capacity. It cannot make unreliable supplier information accurate; its benefit may primarily be fewer premature promises and fewer uncertainty-driven calls. Customers needing a date immediately may find the process less satisfying.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Run for four weeks, alternating new eligible jobs between this process and current practice, with both groups receiving honest delay disclosures. Use the past 30 records as context where timestamps exist, not as a complete baseline by assumption. On paper, tally missed communicated pickup dates/windows, inbound status calls and staff minutes for checks, updates and calls; record how many jobs received any pickup estimate and how early. Inspect unresolved jobs at week four separately. The mechanism is challenged if supported estimates still miss as often, calls do not fall, or communication time rises without improved reliability. Check that apparent gains are not solely due to withholding every estimate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Evidence-based conditional ranges from comparable past jobs
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use the shop’s own supply history to express uncertainty as a conditional range rather than treating a supplier’s expected arrival as a certain pickup date. The mechanism is calibration: estimates reflect observed variation for comparable parts orders and include the shop’s remaining repair workload.

Review the 30 job records alongside supplier replies. Where dates are available, write down order, dispatch, receipt and ready-for-pickup dates. Group only genuinely comparable jobs, such as the same supplier and stock status; avoid creating many tiny categories. On a paper reference sheet, show the observed delivery span and the number of examples behind it. Do not describe that span as a guaranteed bound or a statistically established confidence interval. Sparse or inconsistent groups receive “insufficient evidence for a pickup window.”

For each new job, record the supplier’s current evidence and use relevant historical variation as a reasonableness check. Give a conditional pickup range only if the current supplier status, comparable history and workshop capacity support one: “If the dispatched part arrives within the supplier’s range, we expect collection Thursday–Monday; this remains provisional until it arrives.” If supplier evidence conflicts with history, investigate and explain the uncertainty rather than averaging it away. Review affected cards daily and contact customers when the range changes or becomes unsupported. Confirm pickup after parts inspection and scheduling.

One staff member maintains the reference sheet and inbox annotations; the other records communicated ranges and revisions on job cards. This needs no software beyond the inbox. It assumes useful dates and some comparable past jobs exist. Thirty records may be too few, and changing supplier conditions can invalidate historical patterns. In those cases, communicate status and the next update time instead of inventing precision.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For four weeks, alternate eligible jobs between these conditional ranges and the shop’s current honest estimating practice. Log initial and revised windows, misses against the initial window, inbound status calls and total staff minutes. Track window width, lead time and jobs without estimates so broad or late ranges cannot masquerade as better accuracy. Use the historical sheet only where supporting examples are visible. A small falsifying check is whether comparable deliveries immediately fall outside its observed span repeatedly; suspend that grouping if so. Judge the process unsuccessful if misses remain comparable while windows become substantially less useful or staff time increases.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Exception-triggered supplier clarification and delay recovery
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make pickup estimates more accurate by resolving missing or contradictory parts information before it contaminates the estimate. The primary mechanism is targeted exception handling: staff pursue the few supply uncertainties threatening customer commitments instead of treating all supplier replies as equally informative.

Use the 30 past jobs and supplier replies to identify recurring warning signs, such as an order acknowledgement mistaken for dispatch, a backorder without a replenishment date, or an expected arrival passing without tracking movement. These are investigation triggers, not proof that a delivery will fail. On each paper job card, record the current supplier evidence, any supported conditional pickup window, the next supply milestone and the latest time that milestone can occur without undermining that window. Include repair time and workshop capacity when setting that threshold.

At one daily inbox review, one staff member pulls cards whose milestone is missing, overdue or contradictory. Using the existing supplier email channel, ask a specific question: Is this allocated stock? Has it dispatched? What arrival range is currently supported? Request a tracking reference where applicable. If a supported alternative part or delivery option is available, assess compatibility, cost and customer authorization before changing the order; the process does not depend on alternatives existing. The second staff member contacts affected customers as soon as their current window loses support, even if the supplier has not replied. State what changed, what is unknown and when the next update will come. Never retain an invalid window while awaiting clarification.

Implementation needs a handwritten exception list, short email templates and clear daily ownership. It assumes suppliers sometimes provide useful clarification and staff can identify milestone dependencies. Supplier silence, missing records or universal backorders may leave accuracy unchanged; escalation still cannot justify an unsupported date.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Trial for four weeks, alternating new jobs between exception handling and current practice, with equal requirements to disclose known delays. Compare missed initial pickup estimates, inbound customer status calls and staff minutes, including supplier chasing. Record estimate availability, revisions and unresolved jobs. For each trigger, note whether clarification arrived before the threatened window and whether it materially changed the estimate or repair plan. The mechanism is weakened if chasing mostly produces no actionable information, warnings arrive too late, or misses and calls remain unchanged while staff time rises. Inspect several triggered cards against their emails to verify that revised promises have actual evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A protected repair slot for jobs released by arriving parts
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Reduce pickup uncertainty by protecting workshop capacity for jobs whose parts arrive unexpectedly. The mechanism is operational: shorten and stabilize the wait between parts receipt and repair completion, so variable deliveries do not also create an unpredictable workshop queue.

Review the 30 past job cards and supplier replies for any recorded gap between parts receipt and repair start. If that gap is substantial, trial one small, protected repair block on working days. Size it using documented repair durations and the two staff members’ available hours; do not assume historical timestamps exist. Fill the rest of the schedule normally. Until a stated daily cutoff, keep the protected block available for the oldest waiting job whose complete, correct parts have arrived and whose remaining work fits. If none qualifies, release it to ordinary work. Longer repairs require separately available capacity.

Use a paper diary alongside the job cards. One staff member checks arrivals and records remaining work; the other assigns the block and communicates the resulting pickup estimate. Both can cover either role. Before parts arrive, explain that pickup remains unconfirmed and give a next-update time. After receipt and inspection, estimate pickup from an actual available block and a credible repair duration. Record and disclose delays immediately if diagnosis changes or the block becomes unavailable.

This requires no purchased tools, but it consumes scheduling flexibility and may delay other work. It assumes staff control the schedule, enough repairs fit the block, and waiting after receipt is a meaningful source of error. It will offer little benefit where supplier transit dominates the entire delay or every repair requires lengthy, unpredictable work.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare two weeks of current scheduling with two weeks using protected blocks, keeping truthful status updates throughout. On paper, record missed original pickup estimates, inbound status calls and staff minutes spent scheduling, checking and communicating. Also record receipt-to-start time, completed jobs, unused block minutes and estimate availability. Report unfinished jobs separately. Inspect the first five eligible arrivals: if the protected block seldom advances their start, the mechanism lacks support. Four-week differences remain tentative because job mix and deliveries may change; reject the approach if it merely transfers delays to other customers without improving estimate reliability.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Check the whole repair requirement before estimating pickup
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Reduce estimate failures caused by discovering an additional required part after the initially ordered part arrives. The mechanism is an early completeness check: establish which parts and diagnostic dependencies must be resolved for the whole repair, then base the estimate on the slowest unresolved requirement. This could help when individually accurate supplier arrival information still produces inaccurate pickup estimates because the original parts list was incomplete.

Review the 30 past job records and supplier replies for documented additional orders, incompatible parts or repairs that required further diagnosis after dismantling. Use those examples to create a short handwritten checklist for recurring repair types; missing documentation is not evidence that these problems never occurred.

Before ordering, the diagnosing staff member lists required parts, compatibility details and any checks that could reveal further requirements. The second staff member briefly checks that list against the diagnosis and proposed order. Perform only practical, authorized inspections; record dependencies that cannot yet be resolved. On the paper job card, give each required item its own supplier status and mark the requirement that currently controls completion.

Explain unresolved dependencies to the customer. If an inspection must wait until the first part arrives, say that pickup cannot yet be estimated reliably and commit to an update. Offer a pickup window only when the complete repair requirements, supplier evidence and available workshop time support it. Communicate newly discovered requirements and resulting delays promptly.

This needs a checklist, a few extra job-card fields and time from both staff, using the existing inbox. It assumes incomplete diagnosis or ordering contributes to delays and that some omissions are detectable beforehand. It offers little benefit when requirements are already consistently complete or delivery variation alone causes misses.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
For four weeks, alternate new eligible jobs between the completeness check and ordinary diagnosis and ordering, with both groups disclosing uncertainties and delays honestly. Record misses against the first communicated pickup window, inbound customer status calls and total staff minutes, including inspection, checking, supplier correspondence and customer updates. Also record additional orders discovered after the initial order, estimate availability and unfinished jobs.

Inspect the first five checked jobs: did the review identify a necessary item or unresolved dependency that ordinary preparation had missed? Compare subsequent additional-order delays across groups. The mechanism lacks support if checks uncover no useful omissions and additional-order delays remain similar while staff time increases. Treat four-week differences as tentative if volumes are small; do not count withholding all estimates as improved accuracy.

EXPAND.title: Reserve workshop capacity behind each supported estimate
EXPAND.proposal:
Make pickup estimates account for competition between jobs after parts arrive. The mechanism is capacity reservation: several plausible deliveries must not each consume the same repair hours. The prior status-gate process checks workload but does not specify how staff prevent double booking.

One staff member reviews the 30 records to identify usable examples of hands-on repair time. On a paper weekly grid, both staff record available repair blocks after allowing for counter duties and existing work. Each job card shows remaining work and its corresponding reserved blocks. Before communicating a conditional pickup window, staff need current supplier evidence plus space on this grid. If parts status cannot support a window, communicate that uncertainty and a next-update time.

Reservations dependent on deliveries remain visibly conditional. When a delivery slips, release its block for a ready job and reassess the delayed job against the remaining capacity; notify its customer promptly if the previous estimate loses support. Once correct parts arrive, confirm the reservation. Neither employee may promise a window without recording its capacity allocation.

This needs paper, existing email and a short daily coordination check. It assumes repair durations are sufficiently predictable to reserve useful blocks. Highly variable diagnosis and frequent interruptions may defeat the grid; unused reservations can also reduce throughput.
EXPAND.experiment: For four weeks, one staff member owns the grid and both tally missed original estimates, inbound status calls and total estimating, coordination and customer-contact minutes. Alternate intake days between reservation-based estimates and the prior status-gate process, recording all commitments on the grid so comparator jobs cannot consume invisible capacity. Compare similar repair types and record estimate availability, completed jobs and idle repair blocks. First inspect three simultaneously expected deliveries: if their promised work exceeds available blocks, the mechanism has failed in implementation. Stop making conditional reservations if they repeatedly leave usable capacity idle while ready jobs wait; retain honest status updates. Reject the added process if reliability does not improve enough to justify coordination time or reduced throughput.

EXPAND.title: Verify the ordered part against the actual repair before forecasting
EXPAND.proposal:
Prevent estimates being invalidated by receipt of the wrong part. The mechanism is error prevention at ordering, rather than better interpretation or escalation of delivery information.

Review the 30 job records and supplier replies for documented wrong variants, missing quantities or substitutions. Absence of such records leaves the likely benefit uncertain. Introduce a brief paper order check: the diagnosing employee records the equipment identifier, required part identifier or specification, quantity and any compatibility condition. The second employee compares the proposed order with that evidence before it is sent. If identifiers remain ambiguous, request supplier confirmation through the existing inbox and tell the customer that compatibility is unresolved; do not derive a pickup date from that order's expected arrival.

Attach or transcribe the supplier's confirmation onto the job card. Check substitutions against the original requirement before accepting them. After dispatch, use only supported delivery information and realistic repair capacity for any conditional estimate. At receipt, match the delivered item to the checked specification before confirming pickup. If a mismatch still occurs, disclose it promptly, correct the order and replace the unsupported estimate with the current status and next update.

The second employee owns the check; both can swap roles. Resources are existing cards, identifiers already available during diagnosis and supplier email. This assumes staff can establish compatibility without paid lookup services. It will not resolve shipping variability or undocumented equipment variants, and checking may delay ordering near a supplier cutoff.
EXPAND.experiment: Over four weeks, alternate eligible orders between the two-person check and the prior status-gate process with ordinary ordering. Log missed initial estimates, inbound status calls and all staff minutes, including checking and reordering. Also record wrong-part receipts, ambiguous orders and missed supplier cutoffs. Inspect the first five checked orders against their diagnostic evidence and confirmations. Stop requiring the second check for an order class if it repeatedly delays dispatch without identifying consequential discrepancies; unresolved compatibility still requires disclosure. Compare reliability with added checking time and ordering delay. If no compatibility errors occur in either group, report the trial as inconclusive about prevention rather than claiming success.

EXPAND.title: Complete independent repair work while waiting for parts
EXPAND.proposal:
Reduce the uncertain interval between parts receipt and collection by moving genuinely independent work earlier. The mechanism changes the repair sequence, rather than changing how delivery uncertainty is described.

One employee reviews the past records for recurring repairs with separable tasks. For each suitable new job, the diagnosing employee marks a short dependency list on its card: work possible now, work requiring the missing part, and final checks requiring the completed repair. With existing customer authorization, complete safe independent tasks during otherwise available time. Examples might include an already-authorized inspection or preparation step, but eligibility depends on the actual repair. Do not dismantle equipment early if that creates storage, safety, reassembly or diagnostic risks.

Record the remaining work after preparation. Communicate a conditional pickup window only when current parts evidence and capacity support it; explain that preparation is complete but delivery remains uncertain. When the correct part arrives, hand the card to the other employee with the remaining tasks clearly marked, perform installation and required final testing, then confirm collection. If the part is delayed or the diagnosis changes, disclose the effect and reassess whether prepared work remains useful.

This uses paper cards, existing tools and the same two staff. It assumes some waiting jobs contain useful independent work and that spare capacity exists. It offers little benefit when installation dominates the job or preparation must be repeated. Final quality checks must remain intact.
EXPAND.experiment: For four weeks, alternate eligible jobs between early independent work and the prior status-gate process using the usual repair sequence. One employee owns eligibility decisions. Compare missed original pickup estimates, customer status calls and total staff minutes; also record receipt-to-ready time, repeated work, storage congestion and delays imposed on other ready jobs. Inspect one representative task sequence before starting to verify that preparation does not depend on the missing part. Stop early preparation for a repair type after any safety concern or repeated rework, and stop allocating it time when ready jobs are displaced. Reject the route if shorter post-arrival turnaround is offset by extra labor or worse reliability elsewhere.

EXPAND.title: Check the customer's recorded expectation before ending each update
EXPAND.proposal:
Prevent a conditional estimate being understood as a firm collection promise. The mechanism is closed-loop communication: verify the expectation the customer actually takes away. Even accurate parts-status gates can fail if customers remember the earliest date and miss its conditions.

One employee reviews supplier replies and job cards to establish the current evidence. At intake and whenever an estimate changes, the communicating employee gives three short statements: current parts status, the pickup window and its conditions if supported, and the next update time. When no pickup window is supported, say so plainly and provide the next update time instead. Then ask neutrally, 'What collection timing will you plan around?' Correct any mismatch immediately and write the customer's understood timing on the card alongside the estimate actually given. For an in-person customer, show the same short wording on paper.

Both employees use the recorded wording when covering each other's calls. If supplier information later invalidates the window, contact the customer promptly and repeat the expectation check. An unanswered call is recorded as undelivered; it does not establish that the customer knows the delay. Existing contact arrangements remain the fallback.

This requires only job-card space and a brief conversational step. It assumes customers can participate through the shop's existing communication channel. Language barriers, inaccessible calls or repeated nonresponse can limit it. It cannot make deliveries more predictable, and staff must still count actual misses against their original communicated windows.
EXPAND.experiment: For four weeks, alternate new jobs between this process and the prior status-gate process using identical evidence standards. One employee owns the tally. Compare missed original estimates, inbound status calls and total staff minutes, including repeat contact attempts. Separately record expectation mismatches discovered during the check and customer reports of a promised date. Inspect the first five conversations through their card entries: a mismatch must produce a documented correction, not simply a completed checkbox. Stop the added question if it causes persistent customer friction without detecting misunderstandings; continue clear delay disclosure. If calls fall but objective estimate misses do not, report a communication benefit only. Reject the process if any benefit is outweighed by longer calls or frustrated customers.

EXPAND.title: Parts-status gates with ownership until the customer receives the update
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the parts-status gate route by closing its interrupted-contact gap: recording a revised estimate does not mean the customer has received it. Preserve the evidence gates—ordered, dispatched, received and checked, repair scheduled—and give a pickup window only when supplier evidence and repair capacity support it. Otherwise give the status and a next-update time.

At each of two daily inbox reviews, the reviewing employee records changed evidence on the paper job card. If it undermines a communicated window, that employee owns customer notification until contact succeeds or the other employee explicitly accepts the card. Mark an unsuccessful attempt as pending, retaining the old communicated window beside the revised status. Before leaving, the owner either completes contact or hands over the pending card with explicit acceptance; after an interruption, resume from those pending cards. Use the customer's existing agreed contact method and arrange the next attempt within normal shop hours. Never treat silence as acknowledgment or retain an unsupported date.

Use the 30 records and supplier replies to identify useful status fields and ordinary repair time. Resources are the existing inbox, job cards and a small pending-contact stack. This assumes usable customer contact details and time for two reviews. Compared with the source, the added burden is tracking failed contacts; the likely benefit is fewer customers planning around an estimate staff have already withdrawn. Unreachable customers remain a limitation.
EXPAND.experiment: For four weeks, alternate new jobs between the original gate process and this upgrade; both must disclose known delays. One employee maintains a paper tally of missed original pickup estimates, inbound status calls and total staff minutes, including unsuccessful attempts and handovers. Also record estimate availability, notice successfully delivered before the old window, and unresolved jobs. Start by inspecting the first three changed estimates: each must show either completed contact or a named owner of the pending attempt. If ownership is lost, restore it immediately and simplify the pending stack before continuing. Stop the extra handover procedure if it repeatedly consumes time without preventing lost updates; retain honest disclosures. Report communication gains separately from actual estimate accuracy.

EXPAND.title: Capacity reservations with a release rule for silent deliveries
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the capacity-reservation route by addressing deliveries that remain unconfirmed while their reserved repair time approaches. The source releases blocks when a delivery slips, but supplier silence can leave staff unsure when to release them.

Use a paper weekly grid of repair blocks available after counter duties and existing commitments. Review usable repair-duration examples in the 30 records. Every conditional pickup estimate requires current supplier evidence, enough blocks for the remaining work, and a written latest receipt-and-inspection time derived from that work and available capacity.

At the daily coordination check, the grid owner identifies reservations reaching that threshold. If the correct part has not been received and checked by then, release the reservation to a ready job and immediately withdraw the affected pickup window. Explain the delay and give the next update time. If the part arrives later, place the repair into the next genuinely available blocks; do not reclaim time already assigned to another customer. A new conditional window requires fresh parts evidence and available capacity. Both employees can cover the grid, but ownership transfers only when the replacement accepts the outstanding decisions.

This preserves conditional reservations and receipt checks while adding a definite operational boundary. It needs only paper and the existing inbox. It assumes repair durations can support useful thresholds. Compared with the source, it may reduce idle capacity and unsupported promises, but can move a late-arriving job further back; disclose that consequence when first giving its conditional estimate. Where durations are too uncertain, give status updates until the job can be scheduled reliably.
EXPAND.experiment: For four weeks, compare jobs using the release rule with jobs using the original reservation process, assigning them alternately and keeping all work on one shared grid. The grid owner logs missed original estimates, inbound customer calls and total staff minutes, plus idle blocks, ready jobs displaced and estimate availability. Inspect the first reservation that reaches its threshold without a checked part: the block must be released and customer notification initiated. Stop advance reservations for a repair class if thresholds repeatedly prove unusable or cause avoidable idle time while ready work waits; schedule that class after receipt. Treat the shared grid and small sample as limits on causal conclusions. Retain the rule only if reliability or usable capacity improves enough to justify rescheduling and communication costs.

EXPAND.title: Offer a complete essential repair separately from optional delayed work
EXPAND.proposal:
Change the scope of the pickup commitment when an optional part is the only reason an otherwise complete repair must wait. The mechanism is removing a nonessential supply dependency through a customer-authorized choice, rather than predicting that dependency more accurately.

During the existing diagnosis or estimate conversation, the diagnosing employee checks whether the job contains independently useful work that can be completed, tested and safely returned without the delayed item. Use the past 30 records and supplier replies to look for such cases; do not assume they exist. Offer the customer a clear choice only when the separation is technically sound: wait for the whole job, or authorize the complete essential repair now and defer the optional work. Explain any extra charge, repeat visit, lost convenience or effect on function before agreement. Record the chosen scope on the paper card.

For an accepted split, estimate pickup using the parts actually required for that agreed scope and available repair capacity. Do not promise a date if those dependencies remain uncertain. The employee completing the repair checks the agreed scope and final test before confirming collection. If separation becomes unsafe or the essential repair fails testing, stop, disclose the finding and obtain agreement on a revised plan; withdraw any unsupported window immediately. Customers who decline receive the ordinary whole-job status and next update.

This uses the same two staff, job cards and inbox. It assumes some optional work is truly separable and customers value earlier return. Compared with waiting for every ordered item, it can make pickup less dependent on supply variation, at the cost of possible repeat labor and another customer visit. It provides no benefit where all parts are essential.
EXPAND.experiment: For four weeks, the diagnosing employee records every eligible case, whether the customer accepts separation, and the reason for exclusion or refusal. Compare accepted cases with similar whole-job cases where available, explicitly noting customer selection and small numbers. Count missed original pickup estimates, inbound status calls and total staff minutes, including later work and repeat visits attributable to the split. Also record time to usable return and additional customer cost. Before the first offer, inspect one actual task dependency list to confirm that the returned item can pass its required checks without the optional part. Stop offering separation for a repair type after a safety concern, unexpected functional dependency or repeated rework. If no eligible cases occur, report the mechanism as untested rather than beneficial.
